questions.question: Which sites are in scope, and what happens on them?
questions.why: Sets the size of the deal and the risk profile before you ask anything harder. Single small sites lose more often.

levels.not_discussed: Fewer than 2 elements, or no named source
levels.touched_on: 2–4 elements, a numeric present as an adjective, or the observation programme without its actual completion rate
levels.answered: All 5 universal elements and the industry element, attributed, numerics numeric
levels.confirmed: Answered plus a supporting artefact — site list, injury log export, layout drawing — and two elements confirmed by a second persona

questions.test: Could someone else walk the site and confirm this number?
counts: "Three sites in scope; Amesbury is the pilot."
"Supervisors are meant to log 8 observations a month. We manage about 2."
"Nine recordables at Amesbury last year, 12.5 a year across the network."
does_not_count: "Safety culture is poor." (An opinion. Not a fact of any kind, and not usable.)
"They need better visibility." (A future state — “Desired future state”.)
"Injuries cost them a fortune." (Impact — “Quantified impact”, and it needs a number.)
questions.confused_with: “Technical problem”. Environment is the setting. A technical problem is a mechanism failing inside it.
questions.traps: "Multi-site" without the count. Group-level injury rate with no site breakdown. Observation cadence without actual completion.
questions.listen_for: A count and names, not 'multi-site'. Nights and agency labour are where risk usually concentrates.
questions.red_flag: Only one small site, or no site count after two calls. Deals of $40–80K are the worst-converting band.

details.label: Number of sites, named, with country
What each site does (production, DC, cross-dock, store back-of-house)
Headcount per site, and the share that is agency or seasonal
Shift pattern and weekend or night working
Vehicle fleet by type (forklifts, reach trucks, AGVs, HGV movements)
Contractors or third parties on site
[M] Continuous or discrete production; lines or cells in scope
[L] Client contracts per site and renewal dates
[R] DCs only, or back-of-house in stores too

questions.question: Where is the risk, and how much of it can they actually see today?
questions.why: The gap between where the risk is and what anyone sees is the reason Protex exists. It also tells you where cameras go.

questions.question: What do they measure and report today?
questions.why: The baseline every business case is measured against. Without it there is no 'before'.

questions.question: What happens after something is found?
questions.why: Tells you whether they can act on what we surface. Buyers name capacity, not detection, as what holds them back.

levels.not_discussed: None recorded, or only outcomes recorded as problems
levels.touched_on: One problem, entries without “Frequency or volume of the failure” or “Coverage gap quantified”, or wording lifted from the PIC library
levels.answered: Two or more distinct problems, all elements each, at least one with a quantified coverage gap
levels.confirmed: Answered with three or more problems, one confirmed by a persona other than the Site EHS manager, each linked to a root cause and a business problem

questions.test: Can you name the thing that is broken, how often it fails, and what proportion of the time it works?
counts: "Our only source of forklift-pedestrian data is voluntary near-miss cards. Six a month across 400 staff."
"Manual inspections cover 19% of the observations we're supposed to be doing."
"CCTV only gets pulled after an incident, so nobody ever watches 99% of it."
"Nothing tells us whether the guard we installed actually changed how people work around it."
does_not_count: "We had four forklift incidents last quarter." (An outcome, not a mechanism. It belongs in “Business problem” and “Quantified impact”.)
"Safety culture is weak." (Too vague to measure, so it cannot be shown to have improved.)
"They have no leading indicators." (True, but it describes the absence of our product. Say which mechanism produces that absence.)
"Injuries are costing them money." (Impact — “Quantified impact”.)
questions.confused_with: “Business problem”, constantly. A technical problem is a broken mechanism the safety team lives with daily. A business problem is the consequence the business carries. Technical pain moves you down the org chart; business pain moves you up.
questions.listen_for: A named reviewer and hours per week. 'We have the data. We just don't have the capacity to analyze it in time' (Compleat Food).
questions.red_flag: 'No one is making corrective action at this time.' That's an accountability problem, not ours. Also a red flag: 'The team will find time.'

details.label: Where corrective actions are logged, and how many are open
How closure is checked: does anyone verify the fix worked?
Who would review what the system finds, and how many hours a week they really have
How findings reach the people who can change the process

questions.question: What does an incident cost the line?
questions.why: In manufacturing the throughput number usually dwarfs claim cost, and it's the one that reaches a COO.

levels.not_discussed: No figures, or industry benchmarks only
levels.touched_on: Some denominators, or figures we modelled rather than they stated
levels.answered: All three industry denominators present and attributed
levels.confirmed: Answered plus at least one sourced directly from Finance or Risk

questions.test: Is this a rate or a price that they themselves use internally?
counts: "A recordable costs us about $40,000 direct, and our risk team applies a 2× indirect multiplier."
"A 5.66% productivity uplift is worth $644,000 to us."
"Premium is $X, deductible $Y, loss ratio Z%."
does_not_count: "Industry average is $42,000 per recordable." (A benchmark. It is not their number and it will not survive their CFO.)
"Downtime costs us a lot." (No unit, so nothing can be multiplied by it.)
questions.confused_with: “Quantified impact”. These are the inputs. “Quantified impact” is the arithmetic done with them.
questions.listen_for: Their own basis (cost per hour or a productivity percentage). Don't impose ours.
questions.red_flag: Nobody in Operations will share the number: the case stays a safety case.

details.label: Cost per hour of downtime, or the productivity measure they use instead
Insurance or captive cost charged to the plant
Open regulator notices, recent inspections or fines
High-energy exposures beyond vehicles: guarding, LOTO, cranes, confined space, hot work

questions.question: What's riding on client contracts?
questions.why: In 3PL the case is contract retention, so contract value and renewal dates are the numbers that matter.

Safety penalty or exit clauses, and how much safety weighs in tenders
Margin per unit, and how much of it goes on insurance

questions.question: What do claims and turnover cost?
questions.why: In retail, manual-handling claims usually dominate cost, and risk management often holds the budget.

questions.question: Do their cameras see the risk?
questions.why: Camera estates kill more deals than competitors. Find out early whether this is a licence conversation or a capital works one.

levels.not_discussed: Not captured, or camera count only
levels.touched_on: Sourced via EHS or Ops rather than IT/Security, or “Coverage of the named high-risk areas, gaps,…”, “Whether RTSP or an API is exposed” or “Camera ownership” missing
levels.answered: Elements 1–14 plus industry, sourced directly from IT/OT and Camera owner
levels.confirmed: Answered plus an artefact — camera schedule, VMS export, network diagram, site photos — and a feasibility verdict per site

questions.test: Could you write the install order today without asking another question?
counts: "Milestone 2023 R2, RTSP exposed, cameras on their own VLAN."
"1080p IP throughout the pick aisles; the dock is analogue and would need replacing."
"The estate is managed by an external vendor — credentials sit with them, not us."
does_not_count: "They've got cameras everywhere." (A count with no capability. Resolution, RTSP and ownership are the questions.)
"IT will be fine with it." (An assumption, and not sourced from IT — which caps this field at Touched on.)
questions.confused_with: Nothing, but it is the field most often skipped rather than confused. Skipping it is how a deal dies after being named vendor of choice.
questions.traps: A camera count with no coverage map. "They have cameras everywhere" without resolution or ownership.
questions.listen_for: Roughly 1080p at 8–10 fps on the risk areas. Camera coverage gaps came up at 61 accounts in 2026.
questions.red_flag: Entrance and fence-line cameras only. An analogue or banned estate means capital works first.

details.label: Cameras per site, and how many face the floor rather than gates and fences
Make, model and resolution; analogue vs IP
Which of the named risk areas are covered, and which aren't
Recording system (VMS or NVR) and whether we can get a stream

questions.question: Who owns the cameras and the network?
questions.why: If someone else owns the estate, they can stop the deal however good the case is.

What they were installed for
Network: bandwidth, how IT and OT are separated, rack space and power on site

questions.question: What will IT, security and data rules require?
questions.why: IT, security or AI-governance approval was the gate at 89 accounts. IT on the deal is the sharpest sign of a win.

questions.question: What is actually going wrong, in their words?
questions.why: The problem has to be theirs, said by them. One we recognised from our own research doesn't count.

levels.not_discussed: None recorded, or only outcomes recorded as problems

counts: "Our only source of forklift-pedestrian data is voluntary near-miss cards. Six a month across 400 staff."
"Manual inspections cover 19% of the observations we're supposed to be doing."
"CCTV only gets pulled after an incident, so nobody ever watches 99% of it."
"Nothing tells us whether the guard we installed actually changed how people work around it."

"They have no leading indicators." (True, but it describes the absence of our product. Say which mechanism produces that absence.)

details.label: Which process is failing: vehicles near people, PPE or procedure, actions not closing, ergonomics, seeing the floor, near-miss reporting, reporting for leadership, contractors
How often it happens, in a number
Who sees it happen, by role
Evidence they can show: a log, an incident, footage

questions.question: Why does it keep happening?
questions.why: Decides whether we're the right answer at all. If people can't watch it 24/7, we fix it. If nobody acts on what they already know, we don't.

levels.not_discussed: Absent, or a restatement of the Technical Problem (auto-fail)
levels.touched_on: A mechanism named but no ruled-out alternative and no headcount test
levels.answered: All five elements, sourced from the Group EHS lead or IT/OT
levels.confirmed: Answered plus confirmation from a persona other than the champion, and a statement of which specific capability closes it

questions.test: Two questions. If this were fixed, would the technical problem disappear? And would ten more safety officers fix it? If yes to the second, it is a resourcing problem and we are the expensive answer.
counts: "Human observation can't cover 24/7. Supervisors have production duties first, and there's no verification layer over what they log."
"The cameras were specified for shrink and asset protection, so there's no analytics layer and the VMS has no API."
"Our measurement architecture triggers on injury, so anything that doesn't hurt somebody generates no record at all."
does_not_count: "Observation completion is low." (The technical problem restated in different words. This is the single most common failure in the whole model.)
"They don't take safety seriously." (A judgement about people, not a mechanism.)
"They need Protex." (The solution, not the cause.)
questions.confused_with: “Technical problem”. If you cannot state the cause without reusing the problem's own words, you have not got it yet.
questions.listen_for: Capacity is the cause buyers name most: 'That frontline becomes the capacity bottleneck' (Munters).
questions.red_flag: Accountability: they know and nobody acts. We'd be selling data into an organisation that ignores its data.

details.label: The reason, in their words: coverage, capacity to act, accountability, data scattered, or controls bypassed
How it came to be this way (cameras bought for security, team cut, acquisition)
One other explanation they've ruled out, and why

questions.question: Would more people fix it, and would they pay for them?
questions.why: Tells you whether you're competing with headcount on price, or whether headcount is the cost you replace.

questions.listen_for: 'I could hire two more safety specialists' (Munters). Four safety staff at ~£248k per site (Compleat Food).

details.label: Answer to 'would ten more safety officers solve it?'
Answer to 'would you fund them?'
What that headcount would cost, in their numbers

questions.question: What have they already tried, and why didn't it stick?
questions.why: Someone who has spent money and been let down wants it fixed. It also stops us pitching what they abandoned two years ago.

More supervisors or safety staff

questions.question: How aware are they, and who agrees there's a problem?
questions.why: A thin record means different things at different stages. Agreement only counts if two people say it, including whoever owns the number.

levels.not_discussed: Unaware: Problem exists in our analysis, absent from their account
levels.touched_on: Told and nodded: We described it, they agreed. The words in the record are ours
levels.answered: Agreed when asked: Open question, buyer confirmed and added detail
levels.confirmed: Volunteered and quantified: Buyer raised it unprompted with a number attached

questions.test: Did the buyer say it first, with a number, and does the owner of the number agree?
counts: "Our near-miss number is fiction. Probably half go unreported." (volunteered, with a number)
does_not_count: Assent to a rep-introduced framing — only buyer-stated provenance counts
Agreement whose wording matches the pre-call library, because the record then holds our sentence
Agreement from anyone with no stake in the anchor
Silence read as agreement
questions.listen_for: Not yet aware: 'already clean safety record'. Aware: 'probably 50 percent… go unreported'. Comparing: a requirements document or a three-vendor matrix.
questions.red_flag: We described the problem and they nodded. Wording that matches our pitch counts as nothing.

details.label: Where they are: not yet aware / aware / comparing options
The line they said that shows it
Who volunteered the problem with a number, and whether the owner of the number agrees

questions.question: Which number does it hurt, and whose number is it?
questions.why: A problem nobody is measured on doesn't get funded. This finds the owner and the gap between today and target.

levels.not_discussed: None, or a restatement of the technical problem
levels.touched_on: One problem, entries missing “Current value and target”, or any entry with no named anchor
levels.answered: Two or more problems, each laddered, owned by two different named stakeholders
levels.confirmed: Answered plus one problem stated directly by the Exec who owns that anchor

questions.test: Would this appear on an operating review slide with safety never being mentioned?
counts: "Our TRIR is the number clients see at QBR. It's been flat two years and we got scored down in a tender because of it."
"Premium is up 18% and the broker says our loss record is the reason."
"Every incident stops the line, and an hour down costs us £14,000."
does_not_count: "Near-miss reporting is low." (A technical problem wearing a suit. Trace it to the anchor it damages and it becomes valid.)
"Observation completion is poor." (Same. It is “Technical problem”.)
"They want to be safer." (Not a consequence and not a metric.)
questions.confused_with: The anchor. The anchor is the category — four per vertical. The business problem is this account's specific instance of one.
questions.listen_for: 'Safety have a goal to deliver 5–10% reduction in LTI this year, last year saw an 8% increase' (FedEx EU). Audit scores and training completion: no buyer has named these.
questions.red_flag: No owner, or a target nobody can state.

details.label: The metric: recordables, lost time, serious-injury potential, claims cost, a board target
Today's value and the target
The person who owns it
What happens if they miss it, in their words

questions.question: Which business priority does it ladder to?
questions.why: Executives fund their own priorities, not safety for its own sake. This finds the one they already care about.

levels.not_discussed: No anchor named, or no Exec identified
levels.touched_on: Anchor and Exec named but relayed second-hand, “The anchor metric's current value and target” or “Capital threshold” missing
levels.answered: All six elements, with 1–4 sourced from the Exec directly
levels.confirmed: Answered plus the Exec stating the anchor problem in their own words, and their threshold tested against the “The gap” total

questions.test: Have you heard their threshold from them, in their words?
counts: "The COO owns downtime, is held to 96% OEE, and needs 12-month payback."
"She's already got $400k earmarked for extra supervision, which is what we're really competing with."
does_not_count: "The VP of EHS is our champion." (That is “Champion”. A champion sells internally; an Exec owns the number.)
"The CFO will approve it." (Have you met them? Relayed exec intent caps this field at Touched on.)
questions.confused_with: “Champion”. The Exec owns the number. The champion sells in our absence. Sometimes the same person; usually not.
questions.listen_for: 'Safety is the hook in, operations is the meat' (DHL CIO). 'It has to be a stacked win' (UPS).
questions.red_flag: It ties to no business priority: real, but not fundable.

details.label: The business priority it hits: [M] downtime, serious-injury and regulatory exposure, plant insurance cost, standards across plants · [L] contract retention, claims against margin, labour, exposure across sites · [R] claims and loss ratio, labour turnover, brand incidents, standards across stores
Whether the person who owns that priority said so themselves
Their target, and the payback they need
What they're already spending against it some other way

questions.question: What does it cost them, on their own numbers?
questions.why: The business case has to be their arithmetic. Buyers reject our averages.

levels.not_discussed: No figures, or industry benchmarks only
levels.touched_on: A total with no inputs listed, or every input rep-modelled (auto-fail)
levels.answered: Industry primary metric present, all inputs tagged, ≥60% buyer-stated, total sent back in writing
levels.confirmed: Answered plus one input from the Finance/risk directly, and evidence the buyer has reused the number internally

questions.test: Could their CFO re-run this from the inputs and get the same number?
counts: "12.5 recordables a year × $40,000 direct × 2× indirect = $1m annually, on our own claim data."
"Eight investigations a year, 20 hours each, at a loaded rate of $65 — plus 40 hours a quarter building the board pack."
does_not_count: "Significant cost." (No number.)
"Industry data suggests $42,000 per recordable." (Our arithmetic, not theirs. Fails the 60% provenance floor.)
"$1m of exposure." (A total with no inputs cannot be re-run when one variable changes, and it will change.)
questions.confused_with: “The gap”. Impact is what today costs. The gap is the difference between today and the target, minus what the change costs.
questions.listen_for: 'The actual cost of workplace injuries… is estimated at £335k per year' (Compleat Food). 'Theoretical models may not reflect practical reality' (Actylis).
questions.red_flag: Most inputs are ours. Under 60% buyer-stated means it's our case, not theirs.

details.label: Cost per recordable, direct and indirect, on their numbers
Downtime or output lost
Hours spent on observations, investigations and safety reporting
Insurance: premium, deductible, renewal movement
Damage to racking, vehicles and product
Fines and regulator response
Absence cover and turnover
Share of these figures the buyer gave us (aim for 60%+)

questions.question: Why now?
questions.why: Stable problems don't create deadlines. A date they're organising around is what turns interest into a decision.

levels.not_discussed: Fewer than 3 elements
levels.touched_on: 3–6 elements, or a compelling date asserted without a reason it binds
levels.answered: All 8 elements plus the industry element, attributed
levels.confirmed: Answered plus the compelling date corroborated by a second persona and prior-attempt outcomes in the buyer's words

questions.test: Is this date theirs, and can they say what happens if it slips?
counts: "Board safety review is in November and I present at it."
"Sign by mid-April or we don't go live for June, and June is when the line changes over."
"Insurance renewal is 1 January and the broker wants something new to show."
does_not_count: "We're aiming to close in Q3." (Our date wearing their clothes.)
"There's budget for this." (Whose? “Commercial & governance” element 2 asks who controls it, not whether it exists.)
questions.confused_with: “Buying process”. This is when and who. “Buying process” is the steps and how long each one takes.
questions.listen_for: A date someone else set: board target, contract renewal, insurer, regulator. Most triggers are incidents.
questions.red_flag: A date we proposed. 'Why now' blank is a Win-Loss red flag.

details.label: The date, and what happens on it
Who set it (board, client, regulator, insurer, audit)
Open regulator notices or a recent serious incident
Governance calendar: board safety review, audit, insurance renewal

questions.question: What does good look like, and by when?
questions.why: Turns 'improve safety' into a condition with a number and a date that a pilot can be judged against.

levels.not_discussed: Nothing, or unfalsifiable statements only
levels.touched_on: Targets undated, unnumbered, unpaired to a baseline, or stated as our deployment
levels.answered: All 10 universal and both industry elements, each with a unit and a date, each paired to its baseline
levels.confirmed: Answered plus confirmation this is the target set they are actually held to, and one target that could not be another account's

questions.test: Could this statement be false in twelve months? If nothing could disprove it, it is not a future state.
counts: "Every forklift-pedestrian interaction in the north aisle seen within the shift it happens, by March."
"20% fewer unsafe behaviours on the pilot line within six months, measured the same way we measure them now."
"Detection accuracy at 90% inside four weeks of go-live."
does_not_count: "Better visibility." (Unfalsifiable, so it cannot be the far end of a gap.)
"A proactive safety culture." (Same.)
"Analytics running on 40 zones across three sites." (Our deployment described as their future. It has no unit they are measured on.)
questions.confused_with: “Desired outcome” and “Future business impact”. Future state is the condition. Desired outcome is the capability it gives them. Future business impact is the benefit that follows.
questions.traps: "Better visibility." "A proactive safety culture." "Getting ahead of incidents." If nothing could disprove it in twelve months, it is not a future state.
questions.listen_for: 'Not only data in, but data out, meaning proof the reduction also' (Munters).
questions.red_flag: No number or no date: nothing to judge the pilot against.

details.label: The target, with a unit and a date, against today's figure
How much of the floor they want visible, and by when
What they'll be able to do that they can't today
Who will use it, by role

questions.question: How will they know it worked, and who says so?
questions.why: Deals without written success criteria give the customer an easy way out at renewal.

levels.not_discussed: Unknown, or a pilot assumed rather than established
levels.touched_on: Validation expected but pass conditions undefined, or “Success criteria” not matching “Desired future state”
levels.answered: All eight elements, pass conditions written as conditions, judge named
levels.confirmed: Answered plus “What specifically happens if it passes” committed in writing by the judge, and the cost acknowledged by the Ops leader whose people carry it

questions.test: Is the pass condition written as a condition, and does it match the definition of success in “Desired future state”?
counts: "10 cameras on one line for six months. 20% behaviour reduction and 90% accuracy, judged by Tim and Jacob. Pass means 25 cameras site-wide."
does_not_count: "They want a pilot." (Scope, criteria, judge and duration all missing.)
questions.confused_with: “Pilot & expansion scope”. Validation is how it gets proven. Pilot scope is which sites and cameras, and what happens next.
questions.listen_for: Cencora: ergonomic events down 25% in 90 days from 100; injuries down 10% in 180 days from 14. Sonoco: '95%+ detection accuracy'.
questions.red_flag: No success criteria by Vendor Selection. One AE had a success plan on 1 of 13 accounts.

details.label: Two or three measures for 90 days and 12 months, with baselines
Who declares success
What happens if the pilot passes
Pass or fail conditions: accuracy, relevance, sites, dates

questions.question: How much can their team actually act on?
questions.why: Volume, not detection, is what stalls live accounts. Set the bar before go-live, not after.

levels.not_discussed: Nothing, or unfalsifiable statements only
levels.touched_on: Targets undated, unnumbered, unpaired to a baseline, or stated as our deployment
levels.answered: All 10 universal and both industry elements, each with a unit and a date, each paired to its baseline
levels.confirmed: Answered plus confirmation this is the target set they are actually held to, and one target that could not be another account's

questions.test: Could this statement be false in twelve months? If nothing could disprove it, it is not a future state.
counts: "Every forklift-pedestrian interaction in the north aisle seen within the shift it happens, by March."
"20% fewer unsafe behaviours on the pilot line within six months, measured the same way we measure them now."
"Detection accuracy at 90% inside four weeks of go-live."
does_not_count: "Better visibility." (Unfalsifiable, so it cannot be the far end of a gap.)
"A proactive safety culture." (Same.)
"Analytics running on 40 zones across three sites." (Our deployment described as their future. It has no unit they are measured on.)
questions.confused_with: “Desired outcome” and “Future business impact”. Future state is the condition. Desired outcome is the capability it gives them. Future business impact is the benefit that follows.
questions.traps: "Better visibility." "A proactive safety culture." "Getting ahead of incidents." If nothing could disprove it in twelve months, it is not a future state.
questions.listen_for: Munters set about 80% relevance. Linde's criteria are 'noise reduction and event relevance'.
questions.red_flag: No number: expect inaction after go-live.

details.label: Events per week the team can review and act on
Share that must be relevant for them to keep using it
Who acts, and when in the week

questions.question: Is it worth it on their maths?
questions.why: The honest number: today's cost against the target, minus what the change costs them, including their own time.

levels.not_discussed: No gap computed, or a benefit claim with no arithmetic
levels.touched_on: Delta on one side only, endpoints not matching their source fields, cost of change absent, or ratio uncomputed
levels.answered: Primary gap line present, endpoints identical to source, ≥60% buyer-stated, cost of change complete, ratio above 1:1
levels.confirmed: Answered plus the ratio tested against the Exec's threshold, the buyer restating the delta, and a per-persona ratio with no negative value

questions.test: Are both endpoints the same figures already recorded in “Operations (core)”, “Quantified impact”, “Desired future state” and “Future business impact” — unchanged?
counts: "$644k productivity plus $500k avoided injury cost, against $175k first-year cost including install and our people's time. 6.5:1."
does_not_count: A benefit claim with no cost side. (Half a gap, and the half that flatters us.)
An ROI built from industry benchmarks. (Our confidence, not their incentive. Treated as below 1:1.)
A current value that improved since the last call. (Endpoint drift. The most common way a business case is manufactured rather than discovered.)
questions.confused_with: “Quantified impact”. And note the gap can be negative for one person while positive overall — a works council facing a new liability has an inverted gap, and their yes is not optional.
questions.traps: Ratio above 3:1 on rep-modelled inputs is treated as below 1:1. Below 1:1 disqualifies; 1:1 to 3:1 means either under-sized or genuinely small, and anyone can fill a small gap.
questions.listen_for: 3:1 or better from their numbers.
questions.red_flag: Below 1:1: 'That's equivalent to my total annual cost of injuries' (Compleat Food). Or someone whose consent is needed gets a new liability.

details.label: Annual value of the change, in their currency
Full first-year cost: licence, IT effort, cameras, consultation, training, internal time
Ratio of value to cost (aim for 3:1)
Anyone who takes on a new risk or workload if it goes in (HR, works council, Security, site GM)

questions.question: Who's involved, and how wide is the deal?
questions.why: Breadth is the strongest single predictor of a new-business win. Safety alone doesn't close.

levels.not_discussed: Single contact
levels.touched_on: Roster partial, or the three-population comparison not run
levels.answered: Eight personas named or ruled out, elements 3–7 per buyer, gap counts computed, contradictions flagged
levels.confirmed: Answered plus zero unengaged decision-makers, zero B.I.D. sources not deciding, and the map confirmed by a buyer rather than inferred

questions.test: Can you point at the person who signs, and separately at the person whose reality your business case is built on?
counts: "Tim owns the programme and is measured on TRIR. Per approves capital and has never spoken to us. Jack runs procurement."
"Josh in IT holds a veto and his condition is the firewall review."
does_not_count: A list of names and job titles. (That is a contact list. The buyer map needs role in the decision, influence, and what each one told us.)
"We're multi-threaded." (How many, at what level, and did they contribute anything to the record?)
questions.confused_with: Nothing — but the three-population comparison is the part reps skip, and it is the whole point of the field.
questions.listen_for: Wins: Ops on 48% vs 19% of losses, IT 34% vs 6%, VP+ 72% vs 46%.
questions.red_flag: Two or fewer people: new-business deals win 4–6% whatever else is true.

details.label: An Operations or plant leader engaged
IT or OT engaged
Someone VP or above engaged
Finance or risk engaged
HR, legal or works council engaged

questions.question: Who signs, and have we met them?
questions.why: Naming the signer doesn't move the odds. Meeting and aligning with them does.

levels.not_discussed: No anchor named, or no Exec identified
levels.touched_on: Anchor and Exec named but relayed second-hand, “The anchor metric's current value and target” or “Capital threshold” missing
levels.answered: All six elements, with 1–4 sourced from the Exec directly
levels.confirmed: Answered plus the Exec stating the anchor problem in their own words, and their threshold tested against the “The gap” total

questions.test: Have you heard their threshold from them, in their words?
counts: "The COO owns downtime, is held to 96% OEE, and needs 12-month payback."
"She's already got $400k earmarked for extra supervision, which is what we're really competing with."
does_not_count: "The VP of EHS is our champion." (That is “Champion”. A champion sells internally; an Exec owns the number.)
"The CFO will approve it." (Have you met them? Relayed exec intent caps this field at Touched on.)
questions.confused_with: “Champion”. The Exec owns the number. The champion sells in our absence. Sometimes the same person; usually not.
questions.listen_for: VP or above who owns a multi-site budget. 'A plant manager or site H&S manager cannot sign a multi-site deal.'
questions.red_flag: A manager-level 'signer' (that's a champion, not a buyer). Budget locked: 'we've already locked down budgets for 2027'.

details.label: Name and title of whoever signs above pilot scale
Whether they own a multi-site budget
Whether we have met them on this, and what they said
Whose budget this comes from, and whether it exists this year
Budget cycle and approval thresholds

questions.question: Who is selling for us when we're not in the room?
questions.why: A champion who hasn't been tested is a coach. Test by what they do, not what they say.

levels.not_discussed: Nobody identified, or a friendly contact labelled a champion
levels.touched_on: Named with a personal stake but never tested — classified as coach
levels.answered: Tested at least once and delivered, all elements complete
levels.confirmed: Answered plus tested twice including an Exec introduction that happened, and they have told us one unwelcome thing

questions.test: What did you ask them to do, and did they do it?
counts: "Tim organised the internal sessions, brought his VP in, wrote half the business case himself, and told us our ergonomics support was too weak to include."
does_not_count: "Our main contact is really keen." (A coach at best. Enthusiasm is not authority.)
"He's on our side." (Untested, so recorded as coach.)
questions.confused_with: “Exec anchor alignment”. And note: someone who only ever brings good news is either not close to the decision or managing us.
questions.listen_for: A safety or EHS champion who has been tested wins 83% of the new-business deals where one is flagged.
questions.red_flag: Champion has never done anything that cost them time or capital. A strong signer with a weak champion wins 0%.

details.label: Name, role, and who they report to
Something they've got approved before
Something they did for us between meetings (an introduction, internal data, a meeting set up)
Something they warned us about that we didn't want to hear

questions.question: What does this mean for them personally?
questions.why: People act on personal stakes. It also tells you what they'll defend if this gets hard.

levels.not_discussed: None, or the champion's view only, second-hand
levels.touched_on: One or two personas, or entries missing “Their stated concern or objection, verbatim”
levels.answered: Three personas with all four elements each, from direct conversations
levels.confirmed: Five or more including the budget holder and the consent gate, objections verbatim

questions.test: Does the sentence contain the word I or my?
counts: "If we have a fatality on my watch, my career is over."
"I'm tired of chasing paperwork nobody trusts."
"My honest worry is my people will think this is surveillance."
does_not_count: "They're frustrated." (Whose frustration, and about what specifically?)
"They're excited about the technology." (Interest, not stake. Interest does not fund anything.)
questions.confused_with: “Intrinsic motivation”. Emotional state is how they feel about today. Intrinsic motivation is why they want the specific target they named.
questions.listen_for: 'Worried the program will be judged a failure with personal accountability for him' (ABF Sugar).
questions.red_flag: A motivation we suggested and they agreed to. It won't survive a competitor who asks properly.

details.label: What they personally risk if nothing changes
What they gain if it works
Their honest concern about this, in their words
Why this target and not a higher one, and who it's committed to (board, client, regulator)

questions.question: Who could say no, and what would change their mind?
questions.why: Silent stakeholders with a veto stall deals that look healthy. Find them while there's time.

levels.not_discussed: Single contact
levels.touched_on: Roster partial, or the three-population comparison not run
levels.answered: Eight personas named or ruled out, elements 3–7 per buyer, gap counts computed, contradictions flagged
levels.confirmed: Answered plus zero unengaged decision-makers, zero B.I.D. sources not deciding, and the map confirmed by a buyer rather than inferred

questions.test: Can you point at the person who signs, and separately at the person whose reality your business case is built on?
counts: "Tim owns the programme and is measured on TRIR. Per approves capital and has never spoken to us. Jack runs procurement."
"Josh in IT holds a veto and his condition is the firewall review."
does_not_count: A list of names and job titles. (That is a contact list. The buyer map needs role in the decision, influence, and what each one told us.)
"We're multi-threaded." (How many, at what level, and did they contribute anything to the record?)
questions.confused_with: Nothing — but the three-population comparison is the part reps skip, and it is the whole point of the field.
questions.listen_for: IT and AI committees, Security, unions and works councils, HR and legal.
questions.red_flag: Two buyers disagree on the target, baseline, signer or date, and it's unresolved.

details.label: Each person who can block it: IT, AI committee, Security, union or works council, HR, legal, procurement
What each needs to say yes
Anyone who takes on a new risk if this goes in
Any disagreement between buyers on the target, the baseline, the signer or the date

questions.question: How will they decide?
questions.why: If they're already comparing options against criteria, find out who wrote them while they can still change.

levels.not_discussed: Unknown, or "they're evaluating a few options"
levels.touched_on: Register partial, no weighting, quality unassessed, or criteria we asserted and never confirmed
levels.answered: Every criterion tagged, weighted, owner named, our position recorded, quality assessed
levels.confirmed: Answered plus one criterion we recommended and they adopted, with the buyer able to explain why it matters, and the register stable across two calls

questions.test: Could you predict how they would score a competitor?
counts: "90% detection accuracy, a self-service rule builder, open API to our EHS system, and 12-month payback — in that order of weight."
does_not_count: "They're evaluating a few options." (No criteria captured.)
Criteria we listed for them and they never confirmed. (Us talking to ourselves. Recommended-and-adopted is influence; asserted-and-unconfirmed is not.)
questions.confused_with: “Buying process”. Criteria are the tests. The buying process is the steps.
questions.listen_for: Criteria with weights and owners. Linde's: 'noise reduction and event relevance'.
questions.red_flag: Weaker than a rival on a high-weighted criterion: reposition or walk, don't discount.

details.label: The criteria, how much each weighs, and who owns each one
Whether the criteria came from them or from another vendor
Where we win a high-weighted criterion, and where we lose one

questions.question: What happens between 'yes' and a signature?
questions.why: Most late losses are stalls. Every step with an owner and a duration is a step that can't surprise you.

levels.not_discussed: Unknown, or "it'll go to procurement"
levels.touched_on: Steps partially known, any type left unknown, no durations, path uncomputed
levels.answered: Every type resolved, owners and durations attached, path computed, preferred vendor and MSA both established
levels.confirmed: Answered plus the register confirmed by someone who has run it here before, every can-start-now step actually started, and the path fitting with slack

questions.test: Can you sum the durations and compare against the compelling date?
counts: "MSA negotiation two weeks, InfoSec review three, works council six, board sign-off on the 14th. Legal and InfoSec can run in parallel."
does_not_count: "It'll go to procurement." (One word standing in for the whole path.)
"Legal is reviewing it." (A status, not a returned redline. The canon is explicit on that distinction.)
questions.confused_with: “Commercial & governance”. “Commercial & governance” holds the dates; this holds the mechanics and the clocks.
questions.listen_for: Owners and durations for every step. 'Legal is reviewing' is not a returned redline.
questions.red_flag: Any step still 'unknown' after a verbal yes.

details.label: Every step: legal, procurement, security review, AI committee, works council, capex approval, each with an owner and duration
Whether we need to be a preferred vendor or sign an MSA
Days of steps vs days to their deadline
Any step type still unknown

questions.question: Where does it start, and where does it go?
questions.why: A pilot at the easiest site lands and then stalls. Choose a site that proves something to whoever signs the rollout.

levels.not_discussed: No scope defined, or a pilot assumed rather than agreed
levels.touched_on: Pilot site named but scope, success criteria or expansion direction missing
levels.answered: All eight elements, success criteria matching “Desired future state” and “Validation”, expansion authority confirmed at the Exec's signing level
levels.confirmed: Answered plus the expansion path stated by the person who owns that decision, and the pilot site's representativeness assessed against the estate

questions.test: Could the Exec sign the expansion, not just the pilot?
counts: "10 cameras on the highest-risk line because that's where the recordables are, then 25 site-wide, then the two European plants — Per can authorise up to €250k."
does_not_count: "Start with one site and see how it goes." (No success criteria, no expansion trigger, no authority tested.)
A pilot at the site with the best cameras and the friendliest manager. (The site whose result generalises least, and the usual default.)
questions.confused_with: “Validation”. Validation is the proving; this is the commercial shape.
questions.listen_for: A representative site the signer cares about. A non-union first site can help.
questions.red_flag: A signer who can only approve one site.

details.label: Pilot site and why it was chosen
Areas, cameras and risks in and out of scope
What would justify a rollout, in their words
Rollout sites, sequence and timing
Whether the signer can approve the rollout at that scale

questions.question: How will the workforce, unions and privacy be handled?
questions.why: The union or works council question decides whether the floor accepts it. Raise it early; it is usually solvable.

levels.not_discussed: Fewer than 3 elements
levels.touched_on: 3–6 elements, or a compelling date asserted without a reason it binds
levels.answered: All 8 elements plus the industry element, attributed
levels.confirmed: Answered plus the compelling date corroborated by a second persona and prior-attempt outcomes in the buyer's words

questions.test: Is this date theirs, and can they say what happens if it slips?
counts: "Board safety review is in November and I present at it."
"Sign by mid-April or we don't go live for June, and June is when the line changes over."
"Insurance renewal is 1 January and the broker wants something new to show."
does_not_count: "We're aiming to close in Q3." (Our date wearing their clothes.)
"There's budget for this." (Whose? “Commercial & governance” element 2 asks who controls it, not whether it exists.)
questions.confused_with: “Buying process”. This is when and who. “Buying process” is the steps and how long each one takes.
questions.listen_for: 'Are you going to coach him or are you going to discipline him?' (UPS). A written memo 'won legal and union acceptance' (Cummins).
questions.red_flag: They want individuals identified: walk away. A union contract bars camera AI and there's no other site to start.

details.label: Sites with a union or works council, what consultation requires, and how long
Whether findings will be used for coaching or discipline, and whether that's in writing
Whether anyone expects to identify individuals
Retention and viewing rules
Monitoring technology introduced before, and how it landed

questions.question: What else are they considering?
questions.why: The real competitor is often doing nothing, hiring, or the EHS platform's own AI.

levels.not_discussed: No alternatives named, or "no competition" recorded
levels.touched_on: External rivals named but do-nothing and internal build unassessed
levels.answered: All elements, with do-nothing and internal build explicitly assessed and rival-to-persona mapping done
levels.confirmed: Answered plus our position stated against every criteria dimension, and every landmine countered with something the buyer acknowledged

questions.test: Have you assessed the status quo as a named competitor?
counts: "Two CV vendors, plus the option of hiring three more safety officers, plus doing nothing until renewal."
does_not_count: "No competition." (An auto-fail. Doing nothing always exists and wins by not being evaluated.)
questions.confused_with: “Exec anchor alignment” element 5 — the competing internal spend is usually the real competitor.
questions.listen_for: 86 accounts named a vision vendor in 2026. Cority, Gensuite and Intelex now ship their own AI.
questions.red_flag: A rival has a head start at a site with more internal pull.

details.label: Other vendors being looked at or piloted anywhere in the group
Doing nothing, building in-house, or adding headcount
The EHS platform's own AI add-on
Anything a competitor has told them about us

questions.question: What would make them sure?
questions.why: Proof bars set after a failed pilot are specific. Know them before you design the pilot.

levels.not_discussed: No risks captured, or risk treated as an objection to handle rather than data
levels.touched_on: Risks named without the proof that resolves them, or sourced only from the champion
levels.answered: All seven elements, each risk paired to a specific proof requirement, from the person who holds the risk
levels.confirmed: Answered plus the Exec's own how-sure answer verbatim, and every risk matched to a proof asset that exists rather than one we would create

questions.test: Does each stated risk have a specific proof paired to it?
counts: "They bought a rule-based PPE system that flagged everything and got switched off. They need to see contextual filtering working on their own floor."
does_not_count: "They had some concerns but I handled them." (Risk treated as an objection rather than recorded as data. It will come back at signature.)
questions.confused_with: “Future emotional state” element 4 feeds this — the residual doubt is the input.
questions.listen_for: 'Weekly weighted accuracy rate reporting' (Pirelli). Earlier trials died at about 60% accuracy.
questions.red_flag: The reference they need doesn't exist.

details.label: The risks they've stated, and the proof each needs
Accuracy and relevance bar, and figures other vendors quoted
Reference they'd trust: same industry, scale, union environment
What happens to them if it fails

questions.question: What will they do next, and by when?
questions.why: A next step on our calendar isn't progress. A next step on theirs, that costs them something, is.

levels.not_discussed: No next yes identified, or rep activity recorded as a next yes
levels.touched_on: A next yes named without “Why this buyer values giving it”, or a map covering only people we have already met
levels.answered: All eight elements, map covering every consent-holder, at least one yes given in the last review period
levels.confirmed: Answered plus a plan for the two yeses after this one, and every refusal diagnosed and acted on

questions.test: Who does the work — them or us?
counts: "He's introducing me to the COO on Thursday."
"She's pulling the claims breakdown by injury type — that's a couple of hours of someone's time."

does_not_count: "I'll follow up next week." (Our activity. The buyer's effort line stays flat while ours climbs.)

questions.confused_with: A next step. A next step is on our calendar; a next yes is on theirs. No next yes means stalled by definition.
questions.listen_for: Any two commitments that cost them time or capital means they're on the journey with you.
questions.red_flag: No next step, or no meeting in three weeks. Meetings and demos alone are the most common false positive.
